A comprehensive bats integration test suite (50+ files) covers shell-level execution semantics from end to end, providing regression protection for bash-compat behavior

test_strategy.issue_character: The codebase has a two-tier gap: the shell execution orchestration layer (engine.rs, orchestrator.rs, repl.rs, control_flow behaviors) is effectively untested despite being the highest-traffic critical path, and the MCP subsystem (connection, pool) has zero unit tests for its connection lifecycle and tool-routing logic.
test_strategy.score_rationale: The codebase scores well on persistence and domain-model unit testing, and the bats suite provides meaningful integration coverage for shell execution. However, the core shell execution entry points (execute_command_with_status, execute_shell_command, the REPL loop) and the MCP subsystem have essentially no test coverage at any level beyond shell-level bats tests. Several existing test modules in critical files (control_flow.rs, background.rs, serialization.rs) are placeholder-quality — they assert constants or a single trivial case rather than exercising the logic. Redirect tests also use shared /tmp paths that cause parallel-run fragility. These gaps place this codebase between the 'has unit tests for data layer but misses critical paths' and 'spotty integration coverage' anchors, yielding a mid-range score.

strengths: The workspace crate split is clearly domain-driven: colony-parser, colony-expand, colony-agent, colony-tuple, colony-protocol, colony-panel, colony-memory each have a legible, well-bounded purpose that a new engineer can explain in one sentence.

colony-agent's 16 modules are each individually focused (approval.rs, cancellation.rs, context.rs, planning.rs, router.rs, token_accounting.rs) and the crate's lib.rs top comment accurately summarizes what the crate does.

The PromptComponent and SidebarComponent trait contracts are consistently applied across all 18+ builtin components in colony-ui-core/src/builtins/, giving that subsystem a uniform, predictable structure.
Focused infrastructure crates (colony-secure, colony-reflection, colony-mcp, colony-recipe, colony-focus) each address a single cross-cutting concern without leaking into others.
The separation of *-bin crates for sidebar panel processes reflects a deliberate boundary between the main shell process and long-running UI processes.
high_level_elegance.issue_character: A small number of crates — most severely colony-exec — act as catch-all hubs that absorb subsystems (file tree watching, flux/TUI rendering, goals, mirror LLM, pane management, sidebar) that belong in separate crates or at least have no stated connection to the crate's documented purpose, while inside colony-ui-core a competing dual implementation of the same file-tree capability exists simultaneously.
high_level_elegance.score_rationale: The project is above the mid-range: the macro workspace decomposition into 20+ named domain crates is genuinely strong and well-intentioned, and most crates honor their stated scope. However, colony-exec's scope has grown to include 8 conceptually unrelated subsystems (19K LOC, docstring gap vs. reality), the dual file-tree implementations within colony-ui-core represent a visible ownership failure, and the DockerStatusComponent's bypass of the reactive subscription contract undermines the architectural pattern the whole prompt subsystem is built on. These are not minor nits — they represent places where a new engineer will be surprised to find responsibilities, and where ripple changes are likely (moving 'mirror' or 'goals' builtins requires touching exec). This sits around 60-65, solidly below a 'well-decomposed' 75+ but well above a disorganized codebase.

strengths: The ModelProvider trait provides a uniform async interface across Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, Colony Cloud, ModelRouter, and ProviderChain — all providers expose the same complete/health_check/provider_name/model_name surface with no deviations in signature

Builder-style configuration structs (AgentConfig, MemoryConfig, ApprovalConfig, ProviderChainConfig) are consistently used across the codebase, each providing a Default impl and chainable with_* methods
Error types are domain-local and consistently typed: each crate exposes its own typed error and a crate-level Result<T> alias, avoiding raw strings at public boundaries
The channel trait hierarchy (Channel, ChannelId, named constants) is coherent — all channel types implement the same write/read/flush/clear contract and all constants are co-located

Persistence stores follow a consistent three-constructor pattern (open(path), open_default(), open_in_memory()) within each individual crate, making them locally predictable even if the sync/async choice differs cross-crate
api_surface_coherence.issue_character: The dominant issue pattern is async/sync inconsistency in the persistence layer and a structural split in the Agent's public processing interface that cannot be communicated by types, combined with minor but repeated parameter-convention drift across otherwise similar APIs.
api_surface_coherence.score_rationale: The codebase scores solidly above the midpoint. Within each individual subsystem (providers, channels, errors) the API shapes are highly coherent and the trait-driven provider abstraction is cleanly designed. The score is held back below the 80s by two structural problems: the persistence layer has no rule about when open() is sync vs async, so a developer integrating three stores will need to examine each one; and the Agent's process()/process_full() split presents two non-obviously-different entry points where the difference — full tool handling — is load-bearing but invisible in the type system. These are subsystem-scope issues, not local nits, and together they create real friction at integration time.

strengths: Prompt component types (PromptComponent implementors) form a consistent family: identical import headers, identical new()/default() pattern, subscriptions() returning Vec<TuplePattern>, render() returning ComponentOutput. Every file in crates/colony-ui-core/src/builtins/ for prompt components follows this without drift.
Naming is uniformly snake_case for functions and PascalCase for types throughout all seed files and their neighbors; there is no camelCase drift anywhere.

The panel binary protocol (sentinel-based stdin/stdout IPC) is coherently structured in both colony-env-bin and colony-filetree-bin, with the same event loop shape, emit_frame helper, and InputEvent matching — the protocol convention is recognizable across sibling binaries.

The tuple key naming convention ('dir_change', 'env_change', 'file_change', 'cmd_complete') is applied consistently across the shell core, ui-core builtins, and subscription modules — the drift is isolated to one binary.
convention_outlier.issue_character: The issues are concentrated in two structural areas: a duplicated subsystem (sidebar panels implemented twice under different directory paths with different type and suffix naming) and a single factual mismatch in a panel binary (wrong subscription key, inconsistent error handling style). They are not pervasive across the codebase but they do create real navigational confusion for anyone working in the UI layer.
convention_outlier.score_rationale: The codebase scores well on in-family consistency — within each area, conventions hold. The drag comes from two intersecting problems: the sidebar subsystem has forked into two locations with different naming conventions (Panel vs SidebarComponent suffix, ComponentLine vs SidebarLine usage), making the ui-core directory non-trivially confusing to navigate. The 'cwd_change' vs 'dir_change' mismatch in colony-filetree-bin means that binary silently never reacts to directory changes — a functional bug rooted in convention drift. This is enough to place the score solidly in the 70-75 range: a developer would trust patterns in one area only to find them contradicted in a nearby sibling subsystem.

strengths: The library/core layer is overwhelmingly Result-based: 3286 result_type uses vs 20 returns_null across src/ — virtually no mixed strategy in the core crates
Custom error types with thiserror are used consistently in the main crates (IpcError, StorageError, ExecutionError, ApprovalError) — no bare strings as error values in library APIs
approvals.rs, ipc.rs, and diag.rs all propagate errors through ? rather than swallowing them at the DB or IPC layer
execute_builtin in builtins.rs converts expansion errors to ExecutionError and propagates them consistently — error strategy is preserved across the builtin dispatch boundary
git_branch and git_status components use a coherent Option return for 'not in a git repo' vs Result for actual failures — a sensible layered strategy
error_consistency.issue_character: The issues are localized and boundary-specific: silent error swallowing appears at persistence-deserialization boundaries (approvals.rs timestamp parse) and at binary I/O entry points (panel bin crates), not in the core library layer where the strategy is very consistent.
error_consistency.score_rationale: The core library layer is genuinely strong on this dimension — close to 90-level consistency — but two patterns pull the score down. The approvals.rs timestamp silent-substitution could produce misleading security audit data without any log entry, which is a meaningful failure in a security-sensitive context. The inconsistency between sibling bin crates (unwrap vs expect for the same serialization operation) is minor but visible friction that a developer would notice. These issues are not pervasive enough to reach 80-level 'recurring friction', but they are concrete enough to hold the score below 85.

strengths: Builtin functions in colony-exec/src/builtins.rs use a uniform builtin_ prefix throughout, making the dispatch table at line 226 immediately readable

Panel binary binaries (env-bin, filetree-bin, gitstatus-bin, etc.) share identical handle_key / emit_frame / render_lines conventions — a reader familiar with one binary can immediately navigate all others
Component interface names (id, render, subscriptions, render_block, handle_action) are consistent across PromptComponent and SidebarComponent implementations in colony-ui-core
Common abbreviations ctx, cwd, ttl, cmd are applied uniformly with no inconsistent expansions found
Domain-specific names like invalidate_cache, clear_stale_approvals, rebuild_preserving_expansion, collapse_or_up communicate intent at the right level of abstraction
naming_quality.issue_character: Naming defects are concentrated at boundary functions where a name promises one kind of behavior (pure read, initialization, setup) but the implementation does another; generic verbs (process) appear at integration seams rather than in domain-core code.
naming_quality.score_rationale: The codebase scores above average for naming: domain-core functions have precise, intent-revealing names and conventions are consistent within each subsystem. The score is held back by a small cluster of boundary-function misnomers (get_ that mutates, process_ that dispatches, setup_ that does nothing) and one asymmetric API pair (process_full vs process_with_cancellation) that forces callers to understand the distinction from context rather than from the names themselves. These are module-scoped issues rather than systemic codebase-wide failures, placing the score in the upper-middle range.

strengths: The feature-gated inner/stub pattern (recipe_config.rs, memory_integration.rs, tuple_bridge.rs) is a legitimate abstraction that isolates optional subsystems behind clean compile-time boundaries without leaking conditional logic into callers

ProviderChain correctly earns its abstraction — it implements the ModelProvider trait and adds meaningful fallback, health-tracking, and cooldown logic that callers genuinely benefit from rather than merely forwarding calls

RecipeLoader and RecipeRegistry are cohesive, focused types with no pass-through inflation: each method performs real work (filesystem traversal, manifest serialization, priority resolution) that would otherwise be scattered
The MCP connection pool (McpConnectionPool) adds genuine value: it routes tool calls to the right server, performs reconnection on failure, and aggregates tools across servers — not a thin wrapper

The expansion pipeline modules (arithmetic, parameter, lib) all accept &ExpansionContext directly and perform real work; the shared context is a necessary carrier for shell state, not gratuitous indirection
abstraction_fitness.issue_character: The codebase has a recurring pattern of thin accessor methods (is_enabled, space(), subscriptions(), connection_state() etc.) that expose inner-type fields or trivially delegate to sub-fields without adding policy, combined with a ShoptOptions string-dispatch get/set that mirrors what typed struct access already provides.
abstraction_fitness.score_rationale: The codebase scores above the midpoint because its major subsystem abstractions (ProviderChain, McpConnectionPool, RecipeLoader, feature-gated bridges) are genuine and pay for themselves. The score does not reach 80+ because there are several recurring thin-accessor and pass-through patterns — ProtocolEmitter as a zero-behavior wrapper, ShoptOptions string-keyed get/set duplicating struct field access, and multiple one-liner delegation methods that expose inner types — which add indirection without leverage. These are concentrated in a handful of files rather than systemic, keeping the score in the mid-70s rather than below 60.

strengths: Core async and error-handling deps (tokio, thiserror, miette, serde/serde_json, parking_lot, tracing) are properly centralized in [workspace.dependencies] with consistent versions
Heavy optional features (lancedb, fastembed, arrow, claude-sdk) are correctly gated behind Cargo feature flags so they are not compiled into builds that don't need them
No competing HTTP clients: reqwest is used exclusively for OpenAI/Ollama providers and Colony Cloud SDK with no overlap from other HTTP abstractions
No competing async runtimes or executor libraries: tokio is the single async runtime across all crates
dependency_health.issue_character: The workspace has a split-level dependency management problem: some frequently-used deps are properly centralized while others (rusqlite, chrono, uuid, toml, sha2/hex, dirs) are copy-pasted across up to 8 crate Cargo.tomls with minor version drift, and the workspace itself carries two zombie entries (signal-hook-tokio, rmp-serde) that no crate actually pulls in.
dependency_health.score_rationale: The codebase sits below the average band (65-75). Core framework deps are well-managed, but the per-crate repetition of rusqlite (6 times, with bundled SQLite compiled each time), chrono (8 times), and uuid (8 times with three different pin levels: 1, 1.6, 1.10) indicates that workspace centralization was started but not applied consistently. The two genuine problem findings — zombie workspace deps and `tera` for trivial string templating — are concrete, actionable issues that drag the score further: zombie entries mislead developers about the dependency surface, and `tera` imports a full template engine with 15+ transitive deps for a task that needs no more than `format!` macros. The `term_size`/`terminal_size` dual declaration in colony-shell is a direct two-libs-for-same-purpose violation per the rubric.

strengths: Core data structures (ExpansionContext, GoalTree, RecipeRegistry) are well-bounded — state mutation is explicit and each struct manages its own persistence without leaking internals.
The ControlFlow enum and its propagation through execute_statement_with_control provide a direct, intention-revealing model for break/continue/return/exit semantics.
InputEditor.apply_action is a clean, exhaustive dispatch that delegates each KeyAction to a focused buffer method — state mutation is bounded to the buffer and mode fields.
Helper extraction is consistently used in execution-heavy modules: pipeline segments, guard splitting, and normalization are each pulled into named functions rather than inlined.
The arithmetic evaluator, despite its manual loop, clearly separates tokenisation, precedence parsing, and evaluation into distinct phases with well-named functions.
low_level_elegance.issue_character: The primary recurring weakness is copy-paste control flow: the same error-mapping and early-exit pattern is stamped into five or more match arms in control_flow.rs, the same ShoptOptions string-dispatch is duplicated between get/set, and the same agent-config snippet is repeated across two methods — suggesting that extract-helper discipline breaks down under pressure in the larger files.
low_level_elegance.score_rationale: The codebase sits in the 70-72 range (solid but visibly imperfect). The majority of functions are focused and directly stated, and extraction style is consistent within individual modules. However, several high-traffic files (control_flow.rs, context.rs, builtins.rs, arithmetic.rs) contain duplicated blocks or violated style rules that a reviewer would flag in any PR. The nested if-let in maybe_decrypt_value directly contradicts the project's own written style guide, and the five-times-repeated errexit error-mapping pattern in control_flow.rs is a meaningful maintenance burden. These are not minor nits — they would require real effort to fix — but they are concentrated rather than systemic, which keeps the score above the 60-65 band where issues would be pervasive.

strengths: The PromptComponent/SidebarComponent trait boundary is clean: ComponentContext carries all shell state, ComponentOutput/SidebarOutput carry all render output, and data translation to the terminal protocol is deferred to the manager layer rather than scattered across components.
BuiltinRedirectGuard uses RAII to encapsulate the fd-save/restore lifecycle at the builtin-execution seam, making the handoff between builtin code and the POSIX fd layer predictable and panic-safe.

ApprovalManager isolates the two approval transports (OSC widget vs stderr stdin) behind a single request_approval() method; callers do not know which transport is active, and the oneshot-channel plumbing is entirely internal to the manager.

cancellable_stream is a clean composable helper: it wraps any completion stream with cancellation semantics and returns a single typed result struct, keeping the cancellation concern out of Agent's main loop.
AliasExpansionResult enum makes the alias→execution handoff explicit: the caller receives a typed case rather than a mutated command plus an out-of-band flag, keeping the seam easy to pattern-match.
mid_level_elegance.issue_character: Issues are concentrated in the agent orchestration layer and at the builtin dispatch boundary: two parallel entry points have diverged past the point where a developer can trust that both paths stay in sync, and ad-hoc boundary translations (tool-result injection, sidebar inline branch) create glue-code islands that are invisible from the seam interfaces.
mid_level_elegance.score_rationale: The ui-core component boundary and the approval/cancellation subsystems demonstrate genuinely clean seam design. However, the agent layer has two concrete structural problems that directly harm cross-boundary predictability: process() vs process_full() have silently diverged (different accounting, different observation recording, incompatible tool-result formats), and the AgentDefinition→Agent translation is duplicated with subtly different logic. The sidebar inline in execute_builtin() is a smaller but visible glue-code outlier. Against the 80-anchor ('developer regularly encounters awkward boundary translations'), the codebase sits slightly below: the divergence is in a critical path (the agent's conversation loop) and the tool-result injection is structurally misleading (user messages that are not user messages). Score 72 reflects solid foundations undercut by two subsystem-level seam failures that a developer making changes to the agent would directly encounter.

issues.summary: colony-agent depends on colony-exec to obtain AgentDefinition, inverting the intended agent-over-exec layer order
evidence: colony-agent/Cargo.toml line 13: colony-exec.workspace = true (mandatory dependency, not optional)
colony-agent/src/agent.rs line 110: pub async fn from_definition(definition: &colony_exec::special_files::AgentDefinition)
colony-agent/src/agent.rs line 142: pub async fn configure_from_definition(&mut self, definition: &colony_exec::special_files::AgentDefinition)
AgentDefinition is a parsed document type (prompt, capabilities, model spec) — it has no runtime execution semantics and does not belong inside the execution engine
issues.suggestion: Move AgentDefinition (and its siblings ContextDefinition, ToolsDefinition, etc.) from colony-exec/src/special_files/types.rs into colony-protocol or a new colony-recipe-types crate that neither colony-agent nor colony-exec depends on each other to reach. Both crates can then depend on the shared types crate. This eliminates the upward dependency and unblocks using colony-agent without compiling the full execution engine.

issues.summary: colony-exec/mirror.rs directly queries the colony-reflection SQLite database instead of using the published ObservationStore API
evidence: colony-exec/src/mirror.rs line 14: use rusqlite::{Connection, OpenFlags}
colony-exec/src/mirror.rs line 112: Connection::open_with_flags(path, OpenFlags::SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY) — opens reflection DB directly
colony-exec/src/mirror.rs lines 128-175: query_new_observations() re-implements a subset of ObservationStore::by_session() with raw SQL SELECT from the observations table
colony-exec/src/mirror.rs line 218: hardcodes ~/.colony/reflection/observations.db, duplicating ObservationStore::default_path()
colony-exec/Cargo.toml already lists colony-reflection as a dependency (line 17), so the API is available
The struct ObservationRow in mirror.rs is a partial re-definition of colony-reflection::Observation
issues.suggestion: Replace the raw DB access in mirror.rs with calls to colony-reflection::ObservationStore. Add a query method to ObservationStore (e.g., since_timestamp(ts, limit)) if one does not exist, rather than re-implementing the query in mirror.rs. Remove the ObservationRow re-definition. This ensures that schema changes to colony-reflection break at compile time rather than silently at runtime.

issues.summary: Five crates independently implement identical SQLite open/schema/default-path boilerplate with no shared persistence substrate
evidence: All five files implement the same open(path)/open_default()/open_in_memory() constructor triad
All five wrap Connection in Mutex<Connection> for synchronization with identical lock-poisoning error messages
All five call create_dir_all on the parent directory with nearly identical patterns before opening

colony-agent uses AgentError::Conversation to wrap rusqlite::Error; colony-focus uses FocusError::Database; colony-reflection defines StorageError with #[from] rusqlite::Error; colony-secure unwraps rusqlite directly through its own Result alias — four incompatible error wrapping conventions for the same underlying operation

Path conventions diverge: colony-agent and colony-focus use dirs::config_dir().join('colony'), while colony-reflection uses dirs::home_dir().join('.colony'), producing different filesystem locations on some platforms
issues.suggestion: Extract a colony-storage crate (or a storage module in colony-config) providing: a SqliteStore builder with open/open_default/open_in_memory, a uniform StorageError wrapping rusqlite::Error, and a single colony_data_dir() function that all crates call for the canonical ~/.colony/ path. Each existing store becomes a thin domain wrapper around this substrate. This eliminates the config_dir vs home_dir divergence and centralises rusqlite version negotiation.

issues.summary: colony-exec depends on ratatui and crossterm for its flux TUI builtin, pulling UI rendering into the POSIX execution engine
evidence: colony-exec/Cargo.toml lines 43-44: ratatui = '0.29' and crossterm = '0.28' as direct dependencies
These are pulled in by the flux builtin (src/flux/tui.rs) which renders a process manager TUI inline within the execution engine
The directory profile shows colony-exec/src/ at 19,239 total LOC — the largest crate in the workspace — with flux/ adding 1,148 LOC of TUI code
Any crate that depends on colony-exec (colony-agent, colony-shell, and others) transitively compiles ratatui and crossterm even if they never invoke flux
issues.suggestion: Extract the flux builtin into a separate colony-flux crate that depends on colony-exec for execution primitives and on ratatui/crossterm for rendering, inverting the current direction. colony-exec exposes an interface for spawning and monitoring processes; colony-flux implements the TUI on top of it. Register flux as a plugin/builtin in colony-shell rather than embedding it in the execution engine.

issues.summary: colony-channels depends on colony-reflection, placing observation/analytics concerns inside a low-level IPC primitive crate
evidence: colony-channels/Cargo.toml: colony-reflection = { path = '../colony-reflection' } is a direct dependency
colony-channels is a channel IPC primitive (pipes, buffers, LLM channels) — it should be near the bottom of the dependency graph
colony-reflection is an analytics/observation layer that records shell events — it should be at a higher level than IPC primitives
This coupling means every consumer of colony-channels also transitively depends on colony-reflection's rusqlite, async-trait, and chrono stack
issues.suggestion: Invert the dependency: have colony-reflection observe channel events by subscribing to a channel event trait or callback defined in colony-channels, rather than having colony-channels import colony-reflection. Alternatively, move the diag recording logic out of colony-channels into colony-reflection or a dedicated colony-channels-reflection bridge module in a higher-level crate.

issues.summary: ApprovalScope::Project variant is defined but save_approval always writes 'global'; scope is also ignored at check time
evidence: save_approval SQL (line 109): VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3, 'global', ?4, ?5) — scope is a literal, not a parameter
check_approval SQL (lines 87-89) has no WHERE scope clause, so a Project-scoped approval grants the same access as a Global one
ApprovalScope enum is defined with Global and Project variants, listed in SecureApproval struct, and read back from DB rows — but can never be written via the public API
issues.suggestion: Add a scope parameter to save_approval(script_path, script_hash, variable, granted_by, scope: ApprovalScope) and bind it in the SQL. Add a scope parameter to check_approval and include WHERE scope = ?4 (or implement the intended semantics: Global approvals apply everywhere, Project approvals only when the script is inside the project directory). Until both read and write paths respect scope, the feature is misleading.

issues.summary: AuditConfig.enabled and AuditConfig.file are parsed and merged but never read; audit logging is silently inert
evidence: AuditConfig struct defined at config.rs line 31 with enabled: bool and file: Option<PathBuf>
config.merge() propagates audit config (line 98-99)
No code in the entire codebase reads config.audit.enabled or config.audit.file after loading — confirmed by searching all .rs files for 'audit.enabled' and 'audit.file'
issues.suggestion: Either wire the audit log in SecureRegistry.check_access (append to audit.file when audit.enabled is true, recording timestamp, variable, script, decision) or remove AuditConfig entirely to avoid false security expectations. The current state lets admins configure auditing in secure-vars.toml with no observable effect.

issues.summary: granted_by actor is always the magic string literal "interactive" with no named constant
evidence: registry.rs line 191: hardcoded "interactive" passed as granted_by
approvals.rs line 253 (test): also hardcodes "interactive"
save_approval signature accepts granted_by: &str but the single production call site never varies this value; a config-file-sourced approval would also record 'interactive'
issues.suggestion: Define a const GRANTED_BY_INTERACTIVE: &str = "interactive" in approvals.rs and use it at all call sites. If different grant paths (interactive prompt vs. config file import) should be distinguishable, pass the actual source through the call chain rather than hardcoding.

issues.summary: Eight step-narrating inline comments in process_with_cancellation() narrate code without adding insight
evidence: Lines 372-469 of agent.rs contain: '// Persist user message', '// Apply context window management (prune if needed)', '// Build completion request', '// Send streaming request via router', '// Apply cancellation wrapper', '// Record token usage (estimate based on character count)', '// Add assistant response to conversation history', '// Update context estimate' — each is a label above an obvious call
issues.suggestion: Remove the inline narration comments. The method is short enough to read without labels; any non-obvious constraint (why token estimation uses /4, why pruning precedes request building) deserves a WHY comment, not a WHAT label.

issues.summary: Dead placeholder functions remove_quotes() and expand_command_substitution() retained as exported public API with apology docstrings
evidence: quote.rs: remove_quotes() annotated #[allow(dead_code)], returns text.to_string() unchanged, has a 9-line docstring explaining why it does nothing
command.rs: expand_command_substitution() annotated #[allow(dead_code)], has a TODO docstring, returns String::new(); both are module-pub
issues.suggestion: Delete both functions. The architectural reasoning in their docstrings belongs in a module-level comment or ADR. A function that does nothing except justify its own existence is worse than no function at all — callers cannot depend on it and future engineers must re-evaluate the decision every time they encounter it.

issues.summary: Agent::with_config and Agent::with_provider contain verbatim-duplicated constructor bodies
evidence: with_config (lines 186-222) and with_provider (lines 224-269) both contain identical blocks for constructing tools (with auto_approve check), approval, token_tracker (with budget check), and context_manager; the Ok(Self{...}) struct literal is identical in both
issues.suggestion: Extract the shared initialization into a private fn finish_init(router: ModelRouter, config: AgentConfig) -> Result<Self> and call it from both public constructors. This is the obvious refactor that an AI that generated both methods in sequence failed to perform.

issues.summary: ModelRouter's ModelProvider impl is a pure pass-through wrapper with six delegating methods and no added behavior
evidence: Lines 310-334: complete, supports_streaming, max_context_tokens, provider_name, model_name, health_check all forward directly to self.provider.*() with zero logic
issues.suggestion: The ModelProvider impl on ModelRouter is necessary for callers that hold a Box<dyn ModelProvider> pointing to a router — that use case should be documented. If ModelRouter is never used as a trait object and callers always call router.complete() directly, remove the impl and collapse the delegation. If the impl is load-bearing, add a comment explaining why (e.g. ProviderChain accepts Box<dyn ModelProvider> and is given a ModelRouter).

issues.summary: AnthropicProvider and OpenAIProvider both override supports_streaming() to return the same true as the trait default
evidence: anthropic.rs line 134-136: fn supports_streaming(&self) -> bool { true } — trait default is already true
openai.rs line 116-118: fn supports_streaming(&self) -> bool { true // OpenAI supports SSE streaming } — same redundant override with a comment
issues.suggestion: Delete both overrides. The trait default documents the general case; only providers that return false need to override it. The comment on the OpenAI override ('OpenAI supports SSE streaming') is actually misleading — the implementation does not yet use SSE streaming (it uses a blocking non-streaming request per the adjacent TODO comment).

issues.summary: anthropic.rs complete() annotates every step of a four-statement method with narrating comments
evidence: Lines 110-131: '// Build conversation', '// Convert tools', '// Build SDK request', '// Send streaming request', '// Convert Claude SDK stream to our unified stream' precede each line of a function where the variable names and called methods already communicate the intent
issues.suggestion: Remove the inline labels. The method names (build_conversation, convert_tools, send_streaming) are self-documenting. If the caching branch in build_conversation needs explanation, a targeted comment on that branch is appropriate — not a label on every line of the method.

repl_tui.rs line 22: `use colony_tui::{InputEditor, LegacyPromptRenderer as PromptRenderer}` — production shell REPL still routes through the old renderer

issues.summary: colony-exec/src/file_tree/ duplicates the colony-filetree crate with no dependency declared
evidence: colony-exec/src/file_tree/tree_state.rs and colony-filetree/src/node.rs both define `FileNode` and `GitFileStatus` with diverged schemas (colony-exec uses `is_dir: bool, children: Vec<FileNode>`; colony-filetree uses `file_type: FileType, children: Vec<NodeId>, id: NodeId, depth, hidden, ...`)
colony-exec/Cargo.toml has no entry for colony-filetree
colony-ui-core uses colony-filetree; colony-exec rolls its own identical subsystem

issues.summary: SECURE_KEY_CACHE OnceLock freezes keychain result permanently, making it unresettable between tests and unfazed by subsequent env changes
evidence: static SECURE_KEY_CACHE: OnceLock<Option<[u8; 32]>> = OnceLock::new(); at line 23
get_or_init closure calls colony_secure::Keychain::new() which performs OS keychain I/O (keyring crate) on first use
OnceLock never resets; any subsequent change to the keychain or test environment cannot affect the cached value
issues.suggestion: Remove the process-global OnceLock. Instead, accept an optional Arc<Mutex<Option<[u8; 32]>>> key cache in ExpansionContext's constructor so tests can inject a test key and production code can share one instance. If a singleton is truly needed, scope it to a struct held by the Shell rather than a module-level static.

issues.summary: ApprovalManager::default() reads COLONY_TERMINAL at construction time and permanently bakes the result into the struct
evidence: impl Default for ApprovalManager calls Self::detect_colony_terminal() at lines 217-218
detect_colony_terminal() does std::env::var('COLONY_TERMINAL').is_ok() — a live env read captured into a bool
Any code that calls ApprovalManager::default() without having set the env var will silently get a non-colony-terminal manager; tests cannot override this after construction
issues.suggestion: Remove the env-var read from Default::default(). Either always default colony_terminal to false and require callers to call ApprovalManager::new(ApprovalConfig::default().with_colony_terminal(detected)), or provide a named constructor ApprovalManager::from_env() that explicitly reads the env var so callers know they are doing so.

issues.summary: FastEmbedProvider is independently initialized per MemoryStore::open() call, causing repeated heavy ONNX model loads
evidence: MemoryStore::open() at line 63 calls Arc::new(FastEmbedProvider::new()?) unconditionally — no sharing or caching
FastEmbedProvider::new() calls TextEmbedding::try_new() which loads a 22+ MB ONNX model and runs initialization
MemoryStore::open_with_embedder() exists (line 76) but is not used by the standard open() path; the caller cannot easily inject a shared embedder
issues.suggestion: Make the shared embedder the standard path: change MemoryStore::open() to accept an Arc<dyn EmbeddingProvider> parameter (or a factory), and provide MemoryStore::open_with_fastembed() as a convenience that creates one. The application-level code that boots colony-memory should create one shared Arc<FastEmbedProvider> and pass it to all MemoryStore instances.

issues.summary: CloudConfig::with_key() silently reads COLONY_CLOUD_URL from the environment even when called as an explicit-key constructor
evidence: CloudConfig::with_key() at lines 36-43 reads std::env::var(ENV_BASE_URL) inside its body
The function is documented as 'Create config with an explicit API key' — callers do not expect env reads here
Tests using with_key() will silently pick up COLONY_CLOUD_URL if set in the test environment
issues.suggestion: Remove the env read from with_key(). Add a const DEFAULT_BASE_URL value and use it directly. Provide CloudConfig::from_env_url(api_key) if callers explicitly want the env-var URL.
